 Standard time wins out in daylight saving time debate, economist says
 No one clock has a clear economic advantage over the other, but standard time benefits all areas of the country.
 23 Oct 2026 
 Share on Facebook 
 Share on Twitter 
 Copy address link to clipboard 
 Pixabay image. 
 Dark evenings and light mornings versus dark mornings and light evenings.  
 As U.S. lawmakers debate the passage of the Sunshine Protection Act, which would make daylight saving time permanent across the country, a Virginia Tech economist says no one clock has a clear economic advantage over the other.  
 But if Congress aims to choose the one that provides equal benefits for all areas of the country, permanent standard time is the winner, said David Bieri, economist and associate professor of urban and environmental policy and planning. “Generally, areas of the country that have the most amenities, such as access to parks, recreation, cultural activities, and pleasant weather, would benefit the most from daylight saving time, compared to cities that are lacking those qualities,” he said.
 “The clock is shared infrastructure — a public good like weights and measures,” Bieri said. “When the evidence is a coin toss, Washington shouldn't pick the option that once again favors the places that already have the most." 
 In his own analysis, Bieri found the following results when comparing the economic benefits and human impact of permanent daylight saving time versus permanent standard time.
 Economics —  “The benefits are nearly equal. Permanent daylight saving time would provide more evening sunlight, which people value. However, darker winter mornings could negatively affect sleep, health, and productivity, potentially canceling out those benefits,” Bieri said.
 Community comparisons —  “Wealthier, more desirable communities would benefit more from permanent daylight saving time. Communities with fewer local amenities would be more likely to benefit from standard time,” he said.
 Location matters —  “Northern cities and areas on the eastern edges of time zones, such as Boston and Chicago, would generally benefit more from permanent daylight saving time. On the other hand, standard time more generally benefits Southern cities and areas on the western edges, such as Houston and Atlanta,” Bieri said.
 Safety, energy, and crime —  Differences in traffic safety, crime, and energy savings are small and should not drive the decision. “Permanent daylight saving time moves darkness from the evening rush to the morning, rather than removing it,” Bieri said. “A dark evening commute would have to be five to seven times as dangerous as a dark morning one for daylight saving time to be the safer clock.”
 About Bieri 
 David Bieri is an economist specializing in the institutional architecture of international money and finance, with particular expertise in how monetary and regulatory systems generate structural persistence — including reserve currency dynamics, correspondent banking architecture, and financial sanctions design.
